The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA) bases the 30% share on the expectation that SNAP households spend about 30% of their own resources on food. For FY2027 in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia, the maximum allotment runs from $306 for one person to $1,841 for eight. The calculator above works through six steps in this order: Add earned income and unearned income, such as Social Security, to get gross monthly income. Subtract 20% of earned income. Subtract the standard deduction for your household size. Subtract dependent care, child support where your state allows it, and medical costs over $35 for an elderly or disabled member. Subtract the part of shelter costs above half of that adjusted income, up to $769 unless a member is elderly or disabled. Multiply net income by 0.3, round up, and subtract the result from the maximum allotment. The calculator labels its result as conditional because the formula only pays out once a state agency finds the household eligible. When net income lands above the federal net income limit for your household size, the calculator holds back a benefit amount unless you confirm that a state agency has already found the household eligible. For an eligible household of one or two people, FY2027 sets a $25 minimum benefit. The calculator shows that $25 floor on its own line, and it never turns a failed income screen into an award. The calculator covers households of 1 to 8 people in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia. Households in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, or the U.S. Virgin Islands, and households of nine or more, get no estimate here and should use the FY2027 allotment and deduction tables instead. You can copy or download the result with your inputs, and nothing you type is sent to a server. Income and Deductions for the SNAP Benefits Calculator Enter your household's monthly gross income in two parts, earned and unearned, because the 20% deduction applies to earned income. Wages go in the earned field. Social Security goes in the unearned field. Then enter the deductions SNAP allows. FNA lists these for FY2027: A standard deduction of $217 for 1 to 3 people, $229 for 4, $268 for 5, and $308 for 6 or more, which the calculator applies from your household size. Dependent care costs when the care is needed for work, training, or education. Legally owed child support payments, in states that allow this deduction. Medical costs for an elderly or disabled member above $35 a month, when insurance or someone else does not pay them. Excess shelter costs, explained below. Shelter costs include rent or mortgage payments, mortgage interest, and taxes on the home, so put property taxes in the housing field if you pay them. Allowable utility costs are heating and cooking fuel, electricity, water, and the basic fee for one telephone. Some states allow a set amount for utilities in place of actual bills. FNA does not publish one national figure for that set amount, so the utility field starts at $0. Enter only the utility amount your state SNAP agency approves, and do not add actual bills on top of it. Households experiencing homelessness can get a standard $205.66 homeless shelter deduction. The calculator has no field for it, so ask your agency through the SNAP state directory how it applies to your case. SNAP Income Limits Are a Federal Reference SNAP income limits for FY2027 set gross monthly income at 130% of the federal poverty level and net monthly income at 100%, and most households must meet both limits. FNA publishes these limits for the 48 contiguous states, the District of Columbia, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Alaska and Hawaii have higher limits. Net income is gross income minus the allowed deductions from the six calculator steps. The table works as a reference line because state rules can change the result. A household where every member receives Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), Supplemental Security Income (SSI), or in some places general assistance may be categorically eligible. Most states also use broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE), which lets a state align SNAP income and resource limits with its TANF-funded programs. Under BBCE, household income still must be low enough to produce a SNAP benefit. Non-financial rules also apply. That is why the calculator lets you confirm a state eligibility determination when your net income sits above the federal figure. SNAP Benefits for Older or Disabled Members SNAP changes the benefit math in three ways when a household includes a member who is elderly or disabled: The gross income test does not apply. The net income limit still applies. Medical costs above $35 a month that insurance or someone else does not pay count as a deduction. The excess shelter deduction has no $769 cap, so all shelter costs above half of adjusted income come off. Turn on the elderly or disabled setting in the calculator to apply the medical deduction and the uncapped shelter deduction. Households with a member age 60 or older or disabled can also hold up to $4,750 in countable resources, compared with $3,000 for other households. A person 60 or older who cannot buy and prepare meals separately because of a permanent disability may form a separate SNAP household with a spouse. That applies only when the others they live with have income no higher than 165% of the poverty level, according to FNA . The household has no unearned income, dependent care, child support, medical costs, or elderly or disabled member. The second column raises shelter costs to $1,400, and both columns are our own arithmetic on the FY2027 figures. Each added dollar of excess shelter lowers net income by a dollar and the household's 30% share by about 30 cents. Without an elderly or disabled member, the excess shelter deduction is capped at $769, so shelter costs beyond that cap no longer raise the benefit. The household also clears both federal income references. Its $2,000 gross is under the $3,575 limit for four people, and its $856.50 net is under $2,750. These are full-month amounts. If a state finds the household eligible, benefits count from the date the application was submitted, so the first month's payment can differ from the full-month figure. What the SNAP Benefits Calculator Cannot Decide The calculator runs the federal benefit formula and cannot decide whether your household is eligible for SNAP. Only the state agency where you live makes that decision, after an interview and proof of the information you give. The formula does not check these rules: Countable resources, capped at $3,000, or $4,750 with a member age 60 or older or disabled. A home and lot, most retirement and pension plans, and resources of people receiving SSI or TANF do not count. Vehicles count, and each state decides how. Student eligibility, which the FNA eligibility page covers. Work requirements and non-citizen eligibility, which the Working Families Tax Cuts Act changed. The FNA eligibility page says it is being updated with those changes. Household membership. People who live together and buy and prepare meals together form one household, and spouses and most children under 22 count in the same household even if they shop and cook separately. A state set utility amount, the child support deduction, or BBCE limits can change your estimate. It also changes on October 1, 2027, when FNA adjusts maximum allotments, deductions, and income standards for the next fiscal year. If the state denies your application or sets a benefit you disagree with, you can request a fair hearing within 90 days of the decision. You can make that request by phone, in writing, or in person at the local SNAP office. Your Next Step Save your inputs with the calculator's download. Apply through the SNAP agency in the state where you live. Each state has its own application form, and FNA does not process applications or see case information, so use the SNAP state directory to find your state's office, website, or hotline. In most cases, the state agency sends an eligibility notice within 30 days, and a household with less than $100 in liquid resources and $150 in monthly gross income may get benefits within 7 days. Approved benefits load each month onto an Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) card that works like a debit card. SNAP can buy food for the household , including produce, meat, dairy, bread, snack foods, and seeds that grow food. It cannot buy alcohol, tobacco, vitamins, supplements, hot foods, pet food, cleaning supplies, paper products, or hygiene items. Treat the SNAP amount as a grocery fund and keep it out of your cash take-home pay when you plan the rest of your household budget . Run your numbers in the SNAP benefits calculator and take the downloaded result to your state application. Frequently Asked Questions How do they calculate how much food stamps I get? Your state SNAP agency subtracts allowed deductions from your gross income to get net income, multiplies net income by 0.3, rounds up, and subtracts that amount from the maximum allotment for your household size. For a four-person household with $856.50 in net income, that is $1,023 minus $257, or $766 for a full month. What is the minimum SNAP benefit? The FY2027 minimum SNAP benefit is $25 a month for eligible one- and two-person households in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia. Other areas use the amounts in the FY2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) tables . The minimum applies only after a household is found eligible. How much can you get in SNAP benefits? For FY2027 in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia, the most a household can get is $306 for one person, $562 for two, $808 for three, $1,023 for four, $1,217 for five, $1,463 for six, $1,616 for seven, and $1,841 for eight. Households of nine or more can check the FY2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) tables . Subtract 30% of net income, rounded up to the next whole dollar, from the maximum allotment. An otherwise eligible household with $0 net income receives the full maximum. What are SNAP benefits income limits? For FY2027, most households in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia need to meet both the gross limit of 130% of the poverty level and the net limit of 100%. For four people, that is $3,575 gross and $2,750 net. Households with an elderly or disabled member only need to meet the net limit, and states using broad-based categorical eligibility can align limits with their TANF-funded programs. Can seniors get food stamps? Yes, people age 60 or older can get SNAP when their household meets the program rules, and special rules apply to them. A household with a member who is 60 or older or disabled only has to meet the net income limit, can deduct medical costs over $35 a month, and has no cap on the excess shelter deduction. It can also hold $4,750 in countable resources, compared with $3,000 for other households. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. Subtract the monthly contribution from the monthly benchmark premium. A negative result counts as zero. Cap the result at the monthly premium of the plan you choose. Written as one line, the credit is the smaller of two numbers: your plan premium, or the benchmark minus your contribution (never below zero). Income for the 2027 ACA Subsidy Calculator Enter your household's expected MAGI for 2027, the full year you want coverage. HealthCare.gov states that Marketplace savings are based on expected household income for the coverage year. Last year's income is only a starting point: the HealthCare.gov glossary says to begin with your most recent adjusted gross income (AGI) and adjust it for expected changes. MAGI does not appear as a line on your tax return. Build it in two steps: Start with AGI, which is line 11 of IRS Form 1040 . Add untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits, and tax-exempt interest. Leave out Supplemental Security Income (SSI). For many people, MAGI equals AGI or comes close. Take-home pay alone is the wrong input for this calculator. If your pay stub lists federal taxable wages, use that number. If it does not, HealthCare.gov says to start from gross income and subtract what your employer takes out for child care, health coverage, and retirement plans. Self-employment income goes in after business expenses. Some money stays out of the estimate entirely: child support gifts loan proceeds, such as student loans or home equity loans SSI veterans' disability payments workers' compensation Household size and household income follow tax rules. Your family for the credit is you, your spouse if you file jointly, and everyone you claim as a dependent, including dependents who do not need coverage. Household income adds the MAGI of each family member who is required to file a federal return, so a teenager's summer-job pay counts only if that teen must file. The coverage family is a smaller group. The IRS defines it as the family members enrolled through the Marketplace who cannot get Medicaid , Medicare, or affordable employer coverage. Enter the full tax household size and income, and use a benchmark premium that applies to the coverage family. The Benchmark and Your Chosen Plan The benchmark is the monthly premium for the second-lowest-cost Silver plan that applies to your coverage family, and it sets the size of the credit. Your chosen plan's premium, which the IRS calls the enrollment premium, acts only as a ceiling. The calculator asks for both numbers because they do different jobs in the formula. The IRS settles two edge cases for the benchmark. If only one Silver plan is available where you live, that plan counts as the second-lowest-cost Silver plan. If the two cheapest Silver plans cost the same, that shared premium is the benchmark. Tobacco use changes only one of the two inputs. The benchmark leaves out tobacco surcharges, so enter the non-tobacco price. The enrollment premium is the amount you are charged, so a tobacco user enters the higher plan price. The IRS gives an example of both rules. A $900 non-smoker benchmark is used even though smokers are quoted $1,200 for that plan. A tobacco user charged $650 for the chosen plan uses $650 as the enrollment premium, even though the non-tobacco price is $500. The ceiling comes into play when you pick a cheaper plan. If the benchmark minus your contribution is more than your plan's premium, the credit stops at that premium. The calculator has no ZIP code database and no built-in prices. Its $600 benchmark and $550 plan defaults are hypothetical numbers for the arithmetic. When you apply, the Marketplace estimates your credit from your family size, projected income, and other coverage, and the plan prices it shows are the figures to enter here. A Worked Federal Premium-Credit Calculation In our calculation, a two-person household with $50,000 of expected 2027 MAGI, a $600 benchmark, and a $550 chosen plan gets a $268.85 monthly federal credit and pays $281.15 a month. Both premiums are illustrative and come from no ZIP code quote. The arithmetic assumes every other eligibility condition is met. Use two people with $30,000 of MAGI, a $900 benchmark, and a $100 monthly plan premium. Assume every other eligibility condition is met, including that no one is eligible for Medicaid. Income is 138.63% of FPL, the applicable percentage is about 3.58%, and the monthly contribution is $89.61. The benchmark minus that contribution is far more than the $100 plan premium. The credit cannot exceed the $100 plan premium, so the credit is $100 and the net premium is $0. Read together, the two cases show how each input works. Income sets the contribution. When the ACA Subsidy Calculator Does Not Apply The calculator's figure does not apply to anyone eligible for government coverage that counts as qualifying health coverage, anyone with affordable employer coverage, or a household that fails the IRS filing rules. The calculator asks you to confirm these conditions before it shows a credit. Government coverage: a person eligible for Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) , Medicare, or another government program that counts as qualifying health coverage cannot get the credit for that person's Marketplace coverage. Limited-benefit Medicaid that does not count is an exception. Employer offers: an offer for 2027 plan years is generally affordable if the employee's self-only premium share is no more than 10.22% of household income. The test uses the lowest-cost plan that covers at least 60% of expected costs, and family members' offers apply the same percentage to the family premium. Employer enrollment: enrolling in an employer plan, including retiree coverage, blocks the credit even if that plan is unaffordable. Coverage from a former employer, including retiree coverage, can be declined, and the credit may still be available. Filing rules: married couples who file separately generally cannot claim the credit, with an exception for certain victims of domestic abuse or spousal abandonment. A person who can be claimed as a dependent by someone else cannot claim it. A new Medicaid rule starts January 1, 2027. HealthCare.gov says states that cover adults based on income alone may require a monthly work requirement for Medicaid. A person who lost or was denied Medicaid for not meeting that requirement may get Marketplace coverage but will not qualify for savings. Leave eligibility unconfirmed in the calculator to show an explanation instead of a credit. Limited Medicaid works differently. Some programs pay only for family planning, emergency treatment, or tuberculosis services. If your state's program does not count as qualifying health coverage , you may still get the premium tax credit when you meet the income and other rules. The calculator does not evaluate immigration status or state programs. Three facts can reverse an estimate: an affordable employer offer, eligibility for Medicaid or another government program that counts as qualifying coverage, and changes in law or plan prices. The official next step is a Marketplace application . HealthCare.gov says the application sends your information to your state if anyone in the household may qualify for Medicaid or CHIP. It also tells you whether you qualify for savings on a Marketplace plan. Updating Income Before Tax Reconciliation Advance payments of the premium tax credit are an estimate, and your final 2027 credit is figured on your tax return from actual household income and family size. If the advance payments were larger than the final credit, the IRS sets no repayment cap for tax years after 2025. The full difference reduces your refund or raises your balance due, and if the final credit is larger, the difference goes to you. Reporting changes to the Marketplace as soon as they happen lets it adjust your advance payments. The IRS lists these events among those that can change the credit: a lump-sum Social Security or Social Security Disability Insurance payment a taxable lump-sum distribution from an individual retirement account or other retirement arrangement capital gains from selling stocks, bonds, or cryptocurrency canceled debt, such as forgiven credit card debt marriage, divorce, a birth or adoption, or a move gaining or losing eligibility for employer or government coverage Filing a return is required. Anyone with advance payments must file a federal return with Form 8962 , and skipping that return ends advance payments in future years. Plan the premium around a range of incomes. Run the calculator at a low and a high 2027 income estimate, compare the two net premiums, and set aside the difference if your income can swing. Our guide on how to budget with irregular income covers health insurance costs without an employer plan, and you can put the premium in a household budget . The estimate requires a correct benchmark premium and annual MAGI. Take-home pay alone cannot establish annual MAGI. An affordable employer offer, qualifying government coverage, or changed law or plan prices can reverse it. Compare income scenarios in the ACA subsidy calculator, then update your Marketplace application whenever your income changes. Frequently Asked Questions What is ACA subsidy based on? The ACA premium tax credit is based on expected household modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) compared with the federal poverty level for your household size, plus the benchmark Silver premium for your coverage family. The income sets your contribution, the benchmark minus that contribution sets the credit, and the premium of the plan you enroll in caps it. How to qualify for ACA subsidy? You must meet every IRS eligibility condition. Income alone cannot establish eligibility. Household income must fall in the allowed range. Married filing separately generally prevents the credit, with a limited abuse or abandonment exception. No one else can claim you as a dependent. The covered person must enroll in a non-catastrophic Marketplace plan and lack affordable employer coverage. Eligibility for qualifying government coverage, such as most Medicaid or Medicare, prevents the credit. Limited-benefit Medicaid that does not count as qualifying coverage is an exception. The covered person must pay the share of premiums the credit does not cover. What is the maximum ACA subsidy? The ACA subsidy can be as large as the full premium of the plan you enroll in, because the IRS caps the credit at enrollment premiums. Below that cap, the size depends on how far the benchmark premium exceeds your income-based contribution. In our lower-income example, two people with $30,000 of MAGI, a $900 benchmark, and a $100 plan get a $100 credit and pay $0, assuming every other eligibility condition is met. What are the ACA subsidy income limits? For 2027 coverage, the ordinary range is 100% to 400% of the 2026 federal poverty level in the 48 contiguous states and DC. That is $15,960 to $63,840 for one person, $21,640 to $86,560 for two, and $33,000 to $132,000 for four. Alaska and Hawaii use higher poverty guidelines, and income inside the range does not establish eligibility on its own. Is ACA subsidy based on adjusted gross income? The ACA subsidy is based on modified adjusted gross income, which starts with adjusted gross income from line 11 of Form 1040. You add untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits, and tax-exempt interest, and you leave out Supplemental Security Income. For many people the two figures are the same or very close. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. A family that qualifies for both programs can receive both at the same time. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) loads monthly grocery benefits for a whole household onto an Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) card. The Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) serves pregnant, postpartum and breastfeeding participants, infants, and children under 5. It provides specific healthy foods, nutrition education, breastfeeding support and referrals. For a household that fits both programs, the practical answer is to file two separate applications. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA) publishes the federal rules for both programs. Applications go to different offices: a state SNAP agency for SNAP and a local WIC agency for WIC. On This Page SNAP and WIC Eligibility and Food Benefits Eligible Families Can Receive Both SNAP vs WIC Household Rules SNAP vs WIC Food Benefits How to Apply Through the Right Agency The Next Step for Your Household SNAP and WIC Eligibility and Food Benefits SNAP covers groceries for an eligible household, while WIC covers specified foods and nutrition services for each family member who fits a WIC participant category. The table below draws on four USDA pages: SNAP eligibility , what SNAP can buy , WIC eligibility and WIC benefits . Three differences in the table decide which application a family needs: Who qualifies. SNAP looks at the household, which applies in its own state and must meet income limits, resource limits and other program rules. WIC first asks whether someone is pregnant, up to 6 months postpartum, breastfeeding up to the infant's first birthday, an infant, or a child up to the fifth birthday. What the card buys. A SNAP EBT card buys any food for the household at authorized stores, with listed exclusions. The WIC benefit card buys foods on the WIC list at WIC-approved retailers. What comes with the food. SNAP provides a monthly grocery allotment. WIC adds one-on-one nutrition counseling, breastfeeding support and referrals to health and community services, all at no cost to the family. A household with no pregnant, postpartum or breastfeeding member, no infant and no child under 5 has no one WIC can enroll. For that household, SNAP is the program to check. A household with at least one of those members can check both. Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Who it serves Households that meet their state's SNAP income limits, resource limits and other program rules People who are pregnant, postpartum (up to 6 months after a pregnancy ends) or breastfeeding (up to the infant's first birthday), plus infants and children up to their fifth birthday Household definition Everyone who lives together and buys and prepares meals together; spouses and most children under 22 count even if they eat separately Everyone you live with and share income and expenses with; a pregnant member adds one to household size for each expected birth Benefit form Monthly allotment on an EBT card that works like a debit card at authorized food stores Benefits for WIC-listed foods on a WIC benefit card used at WIC-approved retailers Foods and services Any food for the household, excluding alcohol, tobacco, hot foods, vitamins, supplements and nonfood items Specified healthy foods plus personalized nutrition education, breastfeeding support and referrals to health and community services Application route State SNAP agency where you live; interview and proof of information, with a decision notice in most cases within 30 days Local WIC agency in your area; WIC staff complete a free nutrition assessment before enrollment 📣 Building in finance? Advertise With Us → Eligible Families Can Receive Both A family enrolled in SNAP can also enroll in WIC, and SNAP receipt may already satisfy the WIC income requirement. If you or children in your care receive Medicaid, SNAP or Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), you may already be income eligible for WIC. The USDA WIC eligibility page says those applicants can skip the WIC income chart. Income is only one of the WIC requirements USDA lists. SNAP receipt does not settle the other three: Participant category. The person enrolling must be pregnant, postpartum, breastfeeding, an infant or a child under 5. Location. You apply through a WIC agency in your area, and some areas offer more than one way to apply, including online. Nutrition assessment. Every applicant receives a free, simple health check from WIC staff before enrollment, and WIC uses that information to personalize benefits and services. The California WIC Program states that only staff at a local WIC office can officially confirm that a family qualifies. A current SNAP case can cover the income step of WIC screening, and local WIC staff decide the rest at the appointment. The reverse path works differently. A WIC family that wants SNAP applies with its state SNAP agency. SNAP vs WIC Household Rules SNAP and WIC define a household differently, so the same family can report a different household size to each program. For SNAP, USDA groups everyone who lives together and buys and prepares meals together as one household. Spouses and most children under age 22 who live together count as one SNAP household even if they buy and prepare meals separately. Other SNAP rules affect separate-household status and eligibility for people receiving institutional meals. A person 60 or older who cannot buy and prepare meals separately because of a permanent disability may form a separate SNAP household with a spouse. The separate-household exception requires the other people in the home to have income no higher than 165% of the poverty level. A person who gets most meals from an institution is normally not eligible, with exceptions for elderly and disabled people. For WIC, the household is everyone you live with and share income and expenses with. USDA's WIC page says this includes children, people you are not related to, students away at college, and military service members away on active duty. If someone in the household is pregnant, household size goes up by one for each expected birth. Counting a person in the WIC household size does not make that person a WIC participant. In California, WIC completes a nutrition assessment for each qualifying family member and loads food benefits for those qualifying members onto the California WIC Card. Household size sets the income limit in both programs. USDA sets the SNAP gross monthly income limit at 130% of poverty for applications from Oct. 1, 2026, through Sept. 30, 2027. In the 48 contiguous states, the District of Columbia, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands, that limit is $2,345 for two people, $2,960 for three and $3,575 for four, with higher limits in Alaska and Hawaii. Most SNAP households must also pass a net income test after deductions such as 20% of earned income, a standard deduction and dependent care costs needed for work, training or education. WIC counts household income before deductions or taxes, including wages and tips, Social Security, child support, unemployment benefits and retirement payments. WIC leaves out loans, AmeriCorps income and certain military pay such as Basic Allowance for Housing and combat pay. The USDA WIC page shows income limits after you select a household size and state. SNAP vs WIC Food Benefits SNAP pays for food for the whole household, while WIC pays for a set list of healthy foods for each participant along with nutrition services. Both benefits arrive on cards that work like debit cards at approved stores: an EBT card for SNAP and a WIC benefit card for WIC. SNAP can buy any food for the household, such as: fruits and vegetables meat, poultry and fish dairy products breads and cereals snack foods and non-alcoholic beverages seeds and plants that produce food for the household to eat SNAP cannot buy: beer, wine, liquor, cigarettes or tobacco vitamins, medicines and supplements, including any item with a Supplement Facts label foods that are hot at the point of sale live animals, with exceptions such as shellfish and fish removed from water nonfood items such as pet food, cleaning supplies, paper products, hygiene items and cosmetics WIC foods include fresh fruits and vegetables, baby food, milk, eggs, beans and cheese, according to USDA. The California WIC Program also lists whole grains, bread, cereal, juice, peanut butter, soy milk and tofu. The WIC services come alongside the food: Nutrition education: one-on-one counseling with personalized shopping advice, kid-friendly meal planning, tips for picky eaters, and help with food allergies and special dietary needs. Breastfeeding support: connection to breastfeeding support staff for tips and resources. Health and community resources: referrals to services ranging from medical and mental health care to a food bank. Diapers fall outside both food benefits. SNAP excludes paper products, household supplies and hygiene items, and WIC benefits buy foods on the WIC list. How to Apply Through the Right Agency SNAP applications go to the state SNAP agency where you live, and WIC applications go to a local WIC agency, so a family applying for both contacts two offices. USDA's FNA does not process SNAP applications or have access to case information. The SNAP application runs through these steps: Find your state in the SNAP State Directory of Resources . Each state has its own form, and some states accept applications online. Contact the state agency through its website, a local SNAP office or the state's toll-free SNAP hotline. If you cannot apply yourself, you can name an authorized representative in writing to apply and interview for you. Complete an eligibility interview, usually by phone or in person, and give proof of the information on your application. Watch for a decision notice, which in most cases arrives within 30 days. Approved benefits count back to the date you applied. Some households can receive SNAP within 7 days of applying. USDA gives examples such as a household with less than $100 in liquid resources and $150 in monthly gross income. If you disagree with a SNAP decision, you can request a fair hearing within 90 days, by phone, in writing or in person at the local SNAP office. USDA's SNAP eligibility page notes that the Working Families Tax Cuts law changes certain SNAP rules, including work requirements and non-citizen eligibility, and that USDA is updating the page. For details, contact your state agency through the SNAP State Directory of Resources . The WIC application follows a different path: Use the WIC Eligibility Tool or the WIC locator on the same USDA WIC eligibility page to reach a local WIC agency. Some WIC agencies are run by Tribes. Ask the local WIC office which documents to bring. The California WIC Program may ask for identification, proof of address and income, proof of pregnancy, and medical forms from a health care provider. Bring the infant or child if staff ask, and complete the nutrition assessment for each qualifying member. In California, WIC food benefits load onto the California WIC Card at that first appointment and can be used right away. The Next Step for Your Household A household with a pregnant, postpartum or breastfeeding member, an infant, or a child under 5 should check both programs, because enrolling in one does not replace the other. Current SNAP receipt may satisfy the WIC income test. Local WIC staff still confirm the participant category, the local agency match and the nutrition assessment. A household with no WIC category member has no WIC application to file. For that household, the food-assistance step from this comparison is the SNAP application in its own state. A change in family makeup can switch the next step. USDA's WIC eligibility page notes that having a baby, becoming a foster parent or a change in income can affect WIC eligibility, so a new pregnancy or birth puts WIC on the list. WIC no longer applies when the youngest child turns 5 and no one else fits a WIC category. SNAP eligibility continues to follow its own household and income rules. Once benefits start, plan household food spending with SNAP and WIC entered as separate lines. You can also keep food assistance separate in your budget . Check SNAP vs WIC requirements with your state SNAP agency and local WIC agency , then apply for each program your household fits. Frequently Asked Questions Are WIC and SNAP the same thing? No. SNAP gives an eligible household a monthly grocery allotment on an EBT card. WIC gives pregnant, postpartum and breastfeeding participants, infants and children under 5 specific healthy foods. WIC also provides nutrition education, breastfeeding support and referrals. They have separate eligibility rules, separate household definitions and separate applications, and a family can be enrolled in both. Does SNAP or WIC cover diapers? Neither food benefit covers diapers. USDA's list of items SNAP cannot buy includes paper products, household supplies and hygiene items. WIC benefits buy foods on the WIC list, although WIC staff can refer families to community-based services. What does SNAP and WIC cover? SNAP covers any food for the household, including fruits, vegetables, meat, dairy, bread, snacks and seeds or plants that grow food. It excludes alcohol, tobacco, hot foods, supplements and nonfood items. WIC covers listed foods such as fresh fruits and vegetables, baby food, milk, eggs, beans and cheese. WIC also includes nutrition counseling, breastfeeding support and referrals to health and community services at no cost. Are food stamps the same as SNAP? Yes. USAGov says the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) was previously known as food stamps. Each month, SNAP benefits are added to an Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) card. Can I receive SNAP and WIC together? Yes, a family that meets both programs' rules can receive SNAP and WIC at the same time. USDA says SNAP participants may already be income eligible for WIC. The person enrolling in WIC still has to fit a WIC participant category, apply through a local WIC agency and complete a nutrition assessment with WIC staff. mainEntity.name: Are WIC and SNAP the same thing?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. SNAP gives an eligible household a monthly grocery allotment on an EBT card. WIC gives pregnant, postpartum and breastfeeding participants, infants and children under 5 specific healthy foods. WIC also provides nutrition education, breastfeeding support and referrals. They have separate eligibility rules, separate household definitions and separate applications, and a family can be enrolled in both.

mainEntity.name: Does SNAP or WIC cover diapers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither food benefit covers diapers. USDA's list of items SNAP cannot buy includes paper products, household supplies and hygiene items. WIC benefits buy foods on the WIC list, although WIC staff can refer families to community-based services.

mainEntity.name: What does SNAP and WIC cover?

acceptedAnswer.text: SNAP covers any food for the household, including fruits, vegetables, meat, dairy, bread, snacks and seeds or plants that grow food. It excludes alcohol, tobacco, hot foods, supplements and nonfood items. WIC covers listed foods such as fresh fruits and vegetables, baby food, milk, eggs, beans and cheese. WIC also includes nutrition counseling, breastfeeding support and referrals to health and community services at no cost.

mainEntity.name: Are food stamps the same as SNAP?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. USAGov says the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) was previously known as food stamps. Each month, SNAP benefits are added to an Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) card.

mainEntity.name: Can I receive SNAP and WIC together?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, a family that meets both programs' rules can receive SNAP and WIC at the same time. USDA says SNAP participants may already be income eligible for WIC. The person enrolling in WIC still has to fit a WIC participant category, apply through a local WIC agency and complete a nutrition assessment with WIC staff.

In an ACA vs Medicaid comparison, Marketplace plans are bought through the Health Insurance Marketplace , while each state runs Medicaid within federal guidelines. HealthCare.gov states that a person in a Medicaid program that counts as minimum essential coverage is not eligible for a premium tax credit or other savings on a Marketplace plan. Limited-benefit Medicaid works differently. A new 2027 Medicaid work requirement can also leave some adults with Marketplace access but no savings. The Marketplace or the state Medicaid agency makes the eligibility decision for each person in a household. On This Page Marketplace Coverage and Medicaid Are Different Eligibility Determines Premium Savings Household Income Is Not the Only Test Applying Through the Marketplace or Your State Rules to Check for 2027 Coverage The Next Step Before Choosing a Plan Marketplace Coverage and Medicaid Are Different Marketplace coverage and Medicaid are two separate coverage paths: one is private insurance with income-based savings, and the other is a public program run jointly by the federal government and the states. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) describes the Marketplace as the place to find private health insurance options, buy a plan, and get help with premiums and out-of-pocket costs for those who are eligible. Monthly premiums for a Marketplace plan go directly to the insurance company, not to the Marketplace. Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) provide free or low-cost coverage to eligible low-income adults, families and children, pregnant women, the elderly, and people with disabilities, according to HealthCare.gov. Medicaid programs must follow federal guidelines, but eligible income levels, coverage and costs differ from state to state. Some Medicaid programs pay for care directly, and others use private insurance companies to provide Medicaid coverage. Benefits also follow different rules. Medicaid benefits differ by state, though HealthCare.gov says all states provide comprehensive coverage. Every Marketplace plan covers 10 benefit categories, including prescription drugs, emergency services, hospitalization, laboratory services, and mental health and substance use disorder services, along with pre-existing conditions and free preventive services from in-network providers. Both paths count as qualifying health coverage. HealthCare.gov lists Marketplace plans, Medicaid and CHIP among the coverage types that meet the law's minimum requirements for comprehensive health coverage. ACA Marketplace Coverage Medicaid What it is and who runs it Private health insurance sold through the Health Insurance Marketplace, where buyers compare plans and apply for help with costs Public coverage run jointly by the federal government and each state, with state-set income levels, coverage and costs inside federal guidelines Who can enroll People who live in the U.S., are U.S. citizens or nationals or lawfully present, and are not incarcerated Eligible low-income people; states weigh income, household size, family status, disability, age and other factors Help with costs Premium tax credit and extra savings on deductibles, copayments and coinsurance, based on expected household income and other criteria Free or low-cost coverage; full-benefit Medicaid eligibility rules out Marketplace premium savings How to apply Marketplace application online, by phone, with local help, through an agent or broker, through certified enrollment partner websites, or on paper A Marketplace application, which forwards likely-eligible applicants to the state, or a direct application to the state Medicaid agency When to enroll Open Enrollment from November 1 to January 15, or a Special Enrollment Period after a qualifying life change Any time of year, with coverage that can start immediately 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Eligibility Determines Premium Savings Eligibility for full-benefit Medicaid generally prevents a person from receiving federal premium savings on a Marketplace plan. The IRS lists this as a premium tax credit condition: the person enrolled in Marketplace coverage must not be eligible for coverage through a government program such as Medicaid or CHIP. HealthCare.gov puts it plainly: "If you qualify for Medicaid, you aren't eligible for savings on a Marketplace plan." Declining Medicaid does not restore the savings. A person eligible for full Medicaid or CHIP who keeps a Marketplace plan pays full price for the premium and for covered services. A child may also lose CHIP eligibility if the family keeps the Marketplace plan. Limited-benefit Medicaid is one exception. Some limited types of Medicaid pay only for family planning, treatment of an emergency medical condition, or tuberculosis services. When a Medicaid program does not count as minimum essential coverage, the person may be eligible for premium tax credits and other Marketplace savings if they qualify based on income and other criteria. HealthCare.gov's Medicaid minimum essential coverage lookup shows, by state, whether a given Medicaid program counts and what action to take. People with limited Medicaid can also fill out a Marketplace application to find out whether they qualify for full-benefit Medicaid or a Marketplace plan with savings. Medicaid status is one of several federal tests. The IRS lists these premium tax credit requirements: Household income generally from 100 percent to 400 percent of the federal poverty level (FPL) for the family size. A filing status other than married filing separately, apart from a special rule for certain victims of domestic abuse or spousal abandonment. Not being claimable as a dependent by another person. No access to affordable employer coverage that provides minimum value for the person enrolled. Payment of the share of premiums not covered by advance credit payments. A timing rule applies when status changes mid-year. If the Marketplace found a person ineligible for Medicaid at enrollment and approved advance credit payments, the IRS generally treats that person as not eligible for Medicaid for the rest of the plan year, even if Medicaid later approves coverage. The IRS still tells anyone who may be enrolled in both Medicaid and a Marketplace plan with advance credit payments to contact the Marketplace immediately. Household Income Is Not the Only Test Household income alone does not decide whether a person gets Medicaid or Marketplace savings, because state rules and personal categories change the result. HealthCare.gov says each state's coverage options consider income, household size, family status such as pregnancy or caring for young children, disability, age and other factors. Some states expanded Medicaid to cover adults below a certain income level, and others did not. HealthCare.gov advises applying for Medicaid even when income looks too high. That advice applies especially to people who have children, are pregnant or have a disability. The federal poverty level is a yearly income measure used for both programs. HealthCare.gov's federal poverty level table lists 2026 amounts of $15,960 for one person and $33,000 for a family of four, with higher amounts in Alaska and Hawaii. Under its general bands, income below 138 percent of FPL may qualify for Medicaid in an expansion state, and income below 100 percent "probably won't qualify for savings on a Marketplace plan" but may qualify for Medicaid. Both programs measure income with modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). HealthCare.gov's income guide defines MAGI as adjusted gross income plus untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits and tax-exempt interest, without Supplemental Security Income. Marketplace savings are based on expected household income for the coverage year rather than last year's income. Self-employed applicants count the income they expect to make from the business after expenses. For income that is hard to predict, HealthCare.gov says to report current income, review the yearly estimate it shows, and update the application as changes happen. A wrong estimate carries a tax cost: for tax years after 2025, the IRS applies no repayment cap, so the full amount of advance credit payments above the allowed credit is added to the tax bill. Members of one household can end up in different programs. HealthCare.gov notes that children may qualify for CHIP even when a parent does not qualify for Medicaid. In many cases, a parent who qualifies for Marketplace savings will have children who qualify for Medicaid or CHIP. Applying Through the Marketplace or Your State A household can apply for Medicaid through a Marketplace application or directly through its state Medicaid agency, and either route can lead to the other program. On a Marketplace application, if anyone in the household looks eligible for Medicaid or CHIP, the Marketplace securely sends that information to the state agency, which then contacts the household about enrollment. The same Marketplace application shows whether anyone qualifies for cost savings on a Marketplace plan. The direct route starts with the state. HealthCare.gov's Medicaid and CHIP coverage page lists contact information for each state's Medicaid agency. A state denial feeds back into the Marketplace. In most cases, the state securely sends the person's contact information to the Marketplace, which mails a letter about Marketplace coverage. A denied applicant can apply and enroll in Marketplace coverage without waiting for that letter. Enrollment timing differs between the two: **Medicaid and CHIP:** apply any time of year, and coverage can start immediately. **Marketplace Open Enrollment:** November 1 to January 15. Enroll by December 15 for coverage that starts January 1, or by January 15 for coverage that starts February 1. **Marketplace outside Open Enrollment:** a qualifying life change opens a Special Enrollment Period. Medicaid may also help pay for medical care from the last 3 months, even before enrollment. Payment depends on the family's income and medical expenses at the time care was received. Marketplace applications can be filed online, by phone, with help from someone in the community, through an agent or broker, through certified enrollment partner websites, or on paper. HealthCare.gov offers a checklist of what to gather before applying on its Marketplace quick guide . Rules to Check for 2027 Coverage Two rule changes shape 2027 coverage decisions: a Medicaid work requirement in some states and immigration-status rules for full Medicaid and Marketplace savings. Both notices appear on HealthCare.gov's Medicaid and CHIP coverage page and its Marketplace quick guide . Starting January 1, 2027, adults in states that provide Medicaid based on income alone may need to meet a new monthly work requirement to qualify for Medicaid or keep it. HealthCare.gov states that a person who lost or was denied Medicaid for not meeting the state's work requirement may be able to get Marketplace coverage but won't qualify for savings to lower Marketplace plan costs. After an ordinary Medicaid denial, by contrast, HealthCare.gov says a person may qualify for the premium tax credit or other cost savings. The reason for a Medicaid denial therefore matters for the Marketplace budget. A household comparing plans after a work-requirement denial should expect full-price premiums when estimating monthly costs. HealthCare.gov says that due to a law change, only people with these immigration statuses are now eligible for full Medicaid or CHIP coverage: Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR, Green Card holder) Cuban or Haitian entrant Compact of Free Association (COFA) migrant Depending on the state, lawfully residing pregnant women and children may also be eligible for full Medicaid or CHIP. For Marketplace plans, starting January 1, 2027, only certain immigration statuses qualify for savings. People with other statuses may still be eligible for Marketplace coverage without savings. For 2027 Marketplace coverage starting January 1, the enrollment deadline is December 15. Medicaid applications remain open year-round. The Next Step Before Choosing a Plan The next step is an official eligibility result for each person in the household, from a Marketplace application on HealthCare.gov or from the state Medicaid agency. That result answers the ACA vs Medicaid question person by person. Full-benefit Medicaid eligibility removes Marketplace savings, while limited-benefit Medicaid, an ordinary Medicaid denial and a work-requirement denial each lead to a different savings answer. Neither option is the better choice for every household, because eligibility rules decide which coverage comes with financial help. If the result points to a Marketplace plan, compare each plan's monthly premium and provider network in the Marketplace before enrolling. A Marketplace plan starts only after the first premium is paid, if there is one. Keep the current plan until replacement coverage is confirmed. If Medicaid is approved while a Marketplace plan is active, HealthCare.gov says to end the Marketplace plan when Medicaid starts, unless you tell the state agency you want to keep both. Once the premium amount is known, plan the monthly premium alongside other bills, and if income changes month to month, budget insurance with irregular income before you update the Marketplace income estimate. Frequently Asked Questions What is Obamacare insurance? The Affordable Care Act is a law, and Marketplace plans are private health insurance bought through the Health Insurance Marketplace. HealthCare.gov uses the terms Marketplace and Marketplace plan. Every Marketplace plan covers 10 benefit categories, including prescription drugs, emergency services and hospitalization, and covers pre-existing conditions. Depending on expected household income, a buyer may qualify for a premium tax credit that lowers the monthly premium, plus extra savings on deductibles, copayments and coinsurance. Medicaid is a separate public program run jointly by the federal government and the states. What is a coverage gap in health insurance? The cited HealthCare.gov pages do not define a coverage gap, but they describe situations where a person may get neither Medicaid nor Marketplace savings. HealthCare.gov says that in a state that has not expanded Medicaid, a person who is not eligible may have fewer coverage options and, depending on income, might not qualify for savings on a private plan. Its poverty-level guidance adds that income below 100 percent of FPL probably won't qualify for Marketplace savings. Starting in 2027, a work-requirement denial can produce a similar result: Marketplace access without savings. HealthCare.gov still advises applying for Medicaid in non-expansion states, because each state considers factors beyond income. What disqualifies you for Medicaid? No single factor disqualifies everyone, because each state sets its own Medicaid income levels and categories within federal guidelines. Income too high for Medicaid or an immigration status outside the eligible list can block full coverage, and living in a state that has not expanded Medicaid can mean fewer coverage options. Starting January 1, 2027, adults in states that cover people based on income alone may lose or be denied Medicaid for not meeting a monthly work requirement. HealthCare.gov still recommends applying when income looks too high, especially for people with children, a pregnancy or a disability. Is ACA or Medicaid better? Neither is better for every household, because eligibility rules decide which option comes with financial help. A person eligible for full-benefit Medicaid gets free or low-cost coverage there, and would pay full price for a Marketplace plan. A person denied Medicaid for ordinary reasons may qualify for a premium tax credit on a Marketplace plan, while a 2027 work-requirement denial allows Marketplace coverage without savings. Medicaid benefits differ by state but are comprehensive in all states, and every Marketplace plan covers the same 10 benefit categories. Compare actual premiums and provider networks after the eligibility result arrives. Can you have Medicaid and Marketplace insurance at the same time? Yes, a person can keep both, but full-benefit Medicaid means paying full price for the Marketplace plan premium and covered services. HealthCare.gov says to tell the state agency if you want to keep both, and notes that a child may no longer qualify for CHIP if the family keeps the Marketplace plan. Limited-benefit Medicaid is different: a person may still qualify for Marketplace savings based on income and other factors. The IRS tells anyone who may be enrolled in both Medicaid and a Marketplace plan with advance credit payments to contact the Marketplace immediately.
